1.narration: In the year to June 2026, Amazon spent about 169 billion dollars on capex, more than its operations generated.

3.narration: Add Microsoft and the four reported about 539 billion of capex, each on its own definition. NVIDIA booked 278 billion.

4.narration: That is 51.5 percent. No filing says how much of that capex went to NVIDIA. The ratio is a comparison, not a share.

5.narration: In fiscal 2026, one direct customer was 22 percent of NVIDIA's revenue, another was 14 percent. A quarter later the list grew longer.

8.narration: Matched to the June quarter, the ratio read 52 percent. NVIDIA's filing gave the hyperscaler percentage; the four companies' filings gave the capex.

12.narration: Compute delivered about 162 billion and networking about 31 billion. The same filing gives no customer names, only percentages of revenue.

13.narration: Back to late October 2025. Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon each disclosed a quarter of capex; NVIDIA's matching quarter had ended October 26.

34.narration: The four companies' June-quarter capex totaled about 170.1 billion. NVIDIA's July-quarter data center revenue came to 52 percent of that.

36.narration: Hyperscalers accounted for about 48.7 billion of that revenue. AI clouds, industrial and enterprise customers made up the rest.

37.narration: Now the other side of the ledger: cash flow, leases and debt. Alphabet's June-quarter free cash flow was negative 5.9 billion dollars.

43.narration: The debt line from the opening: Meta's long-term debt was 58.7 billion in March and 83.7 billion by June.

49.narration: Last, the budgets. In January, Meta guided 115 to 135 billion dollars of capital spending for the year. Revised outlooks followed.

50.narration: In April both ends rose. In July only the floor moved, leaving 130 to 145 billion as the range.

56.narration: That higher range arrived with Google Cloud's June quarter, when revenue there grew 82 percent and backlog reached about 514 billion.

57.narration: Added together, the four budgets fall between 720 and 745 billion. NVIDIA's own filing sorts customers into categories of its own.
